item.title: More flexible European Union spending needs stronger parliamentary scrutiny
item.description: Proposed changes to the EU budget and how it is approved go too far in marginalising the European Parliament; this shortcoming should be corrected
item.content:encoded:
The Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) gives the European Parliament significant powers in relation to the European Union’s budget. The EU’s overall seven-year budget – the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) – cannot pass without the parliament’s consent, while the parliament acts as co-legislator alongside the Council of the EU in the annual budgetary procedure1. Together with the Council, the parliament thus has the authority to determine how EU funds are allocated.

However, the European Commission’s proposal for the 2028-2034 MFF foresees a new architecture for the EU budget, which would exclude the European Parliament from significant allocation decisions and limit its scrutiny powers during implementation2. This is problematic not only from a treaty perspective, but also because the parliament, as the EU’s democratically elected institution, should help ensure that EU spending serves EU priorities.

The Commission’s proposals would give national governments a greater role in allocating EU funds across priorities. Governments may be tempted to use these funds to pursue domestic objectives, which might not necessarily coincide with European priorities. Given that the EU budget accounts for little more than one percent of GDP, compared with public expenditure of around 45 percent of GDP at national level, it is essential that EU spending remains focused on common European priorities.

In Darvas et al (2026), we concluded that the European Parliament should not be excluded from major decisions on the allocation of EU funds. Here, we explore options for involving the European Parliament in the proposed new EU budget architecture, while respecting the Treaty-based roles of the parliament, the Council and the Commission. In particular, a reasonable balance should be struck between ensuring meaningful European Parliament involvement and avoiding unnecessary delays in the budgetary process. While implementing the full set of options proposed in this analysis would be desirable, the objective is to ensure meaningful European Parliament involvement at the various stages of the budgeting and monitoring process.

The European Parliament’s limited role in the proposed MFF architecture

In July 2025, the European Commission proposed a major overhaul for the 2028-2034 MFF: reducing the number of budgetary headings and programmes, harmonising EU budget rules, extending flexibility and strengthening performance assessments. The largest amount of spending would be organised under National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPPs); cohesion, agriculture, fisheries, social, migration, border and internal security spending would be integrated into a single framework, within nationally pre-allocated envelopes (European Commission, 2025).

For the purposes of NRPPs, specific amounts would be earmarked for certain cohesion, agricultural and migration and border management spending. However, almost one-third of total spending via NRPPs would be allocated by EU countries without European Parliament involvement. Moreover, a 25 percent flexibility amount would be left for reprogramming in case of emergency or in the mid-term review, also without European Parliament involvement. Consequently, many substantive allocation decisions that under previous MFFs were more tightly constrained into separate programmes and budgetary structures would shift to the programming and implementation stages, in which the parliament’s role is much more limited.

The NRPPs would be subject to performance-based budgeting, under which disbursements would be conditional on the achievement of specified milestones and targets, rather than on the actual costs incurred. In principle, this approach has considerable advantages (Darvas et al, 2023), but experience with national plans under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) – the main part of the EU’s post-pandemic economic recovery programme – showed significant shortcomings in putting performance-based financing into practice (Darvas et al, 2023; ECA, 2023, 2025; Leino-Sandberg, 2026). While the Commission’s proposed performance framework for 2028-2034 would improve on the RRF framework, its methodology for setting milestones and targets remains insufficiently developed.

Under the proposals for 2028-2034, the European Parliament would have no role in approving or amending individual NRPPs, even though these plans would shape how EU funding is ultimately prioritised and spent. Nor would it have a role in the financial decisions setting out milestones, targets and payout values. Potentially, this would not adequately safeguard the European Parliament’s budgetary prerogatives under the Treaties.

One possible, albeit far-reaching, solution would be to make the European Parliament a co-adopter, together with the Council, of the EU acts that must be adopted to approve each national plan, with these acts also incorporating the relevant financial decisions. This could involve either approval of each plan individually or a joint approval process covering all plans. Major revisions to plans could be subject to similar scrutiny.

However, the European Parliament is not an implementing authority under the EU Treaties and lacks the administrative capacity to scrutinise every national plan in detail. Alternative mechanisms should therefore be considered to safeguard the parliament’s budgetary prerogatives. Instead, we recommend a combination of stronger ex-ante parliamentary influence over major choices concerning spending priorities and financial allocations, scrutiny of major plan amendments, better information access and independent evaluation.

Strengthening the European Parliament’s role before NRPP adoption

Under the Commission’s proposals for 2028-2034, EU countries would have considerable discretion in allocating funding across priorities. Discussions and negotiations between each country and the Commission could significantly influence how EU funding is allocated across EU priorities, while the European Parliament would be excluded from these decisions. This could be addressed by:

  • Specifying minimum and maximum shares of funding for major EU objectives that each NRPP should respect; this would ensure that overall spending on priorities remains within the boundaries set by the European Parliament.
  • Clarifying what it means for NRPPs to “effectively address all or a significant subset” of relevant recommendations related to EU policies (including fiscal, environmental, agricultural and migration policies listed in European Commission (2025))3, in order to limit the scope for interpretation in bilateral Commission-country discussions.
  • Requiring the Commission to aggregate the funding allocations in all draft NRPPs and assess how the 27 plans collectively contribute to spending areas; this would allow the European Parliament to assess whether the planned allocations are in line with EU priorities. Particular attention should be paid to cross-border projects, which are crucial for European added value, but were largely neglected in national plans under the RRF despite being well suited for RRF financing (ECA, 2022).

This aggregate assessment should take place sufficiently early to allow the findings to be taken into account in final NRPPs. For example, EU countries could be required to submit draft plans at least six months before the deadline for final plans. The Commission would then have one month to assess the aggregate allocations, followed by one month for the European Parliament to express its views. This would leave EU countries and the Commission four months to discuss and incorporate possible revisions before the final plans are submitted. The parliament’s opinion might not be binding, but the Commission should be required to explain how the parliament’s observations were taken into account in the finalisation of NRPPs4.

Under the Commission’s 2028-2034 MFF proposals, the Commission would assess the (final) NRPPs and propose Council sign-off decisions (‘implementing decisions’ in EU jargon), with no option for the European Parliament to intervene at any procedural stage. This process could be strengthened by:

  • Requiring the Commission to transmit to the parliament before formally submitting a proposal for a Council decision its preliminary assessment of each final NRPP, including a summary of the Commission’s exchanges with the country concerned and the proposed milestones, targets and payout values. The parliament could then be given, for example, one month to provide a non-binding opinion. The Commission should be required to explain how it has taken the parliament’s opinion into account before submitting its proposal to the Council. The Council sign-off decision should include the milestones, targets and payout values.

In scrutinising NRPPs, the European Parliament would also benefit from independent assessments of the NRRPs, the Commission’s assessments of NRRPs and the results achieved (Darvas et al, 2026). The Commission’s close involvement in the design and implementation of NRPPs could compromise its ability to provide fully objective assessments, as was the case with the RRF (Darvas et al, 2025). Independent scrutiny could be provided by an Independent NRPP Evaluation Panel, selected through a competitive process and insulated from both national managing authorities and the Commission services responsible for NRPP implementation. The panel would complement, rather than duplicate, the work of the European Court of Auditors (ECA), by providing systematic assessments of NRPP design, implementation and results, while ECA would retain its independent external audit and evaluation functions. We therefore recommend:

  • Establish an Independent NRPP Evaluation Panel whose assessments would be made public, providing additional evidence for parliamentary scrutiny.

The Council may reject a draft NRPP approval proposed by the Commission. This should trigger the same procedure as for the initial plan:

  • When the Council rejects a proposed NRPP sign-off decision and the Commission submits a new draft decision, potentially after the country concerned has revised its NRPP, the European Parliament should again be able to express its opinion.

Strengthening the European Parliament’s role during NRPP implementation

The Commission’s proposal would allow the European Parliament only a very limited role during implementation of the NRPPs. The parliament would be able to object to Commission decisions on revising six articles and five annexes of the NRPP regulation (European Commission, 2025), or to revoke the Commission’s power to adopt such decisions. The Commission would also be required to communicate information on irregularities to the parliament. However, the parliament would have no role in other implementation-related dialogues, or in the programming of the 25 percent flexibility amount. Moreover, there would be no regular implementation dialogue between the Commission and the parliament, though a comparable mechanism – the ‘recovery and resilience dialogue’ – is in place for the RRF5. At the time of writing, 23 such RRF dialogues have been held (Loi et al, 2026). These shortcomings in monitoring of implementation could be addressed by:

  • Setting rules constraining transfers between fundamentally different policy objectives during implementation. This would limit the scope for substantial changes in spending priorities without parliamentary involvement.
  • Establishing a regular NRPP scrutiny dialogue between the European Parliament and the Commission. At regular intervals, for example every six or twelve months, the Commission should prepare an NRPP implementation report and present it to the parliament. The report would cover payments, suspensions and corrective decisions; amendments to NRPPs; programming of the crisis and mid-term review components of the flexibility amount; conclusions of national monitoring committees; audit findings and remedial actions; and cross-country comparison of implementation. Following each dialogue, the parliament could submit written observations to which the Commission would be required to respond.
  • Major amendments to plans and the intended programming of the flexibility amount ahead of the mid-term review should be subject to prior European Parliament scrutiny, similarly to the scrutiny we propose for initial NRPPs. The parliament should be able to provide opinions on aggregate reallocations, particularly if several EU countries amend their plans at the same time, and on major amendments to individual plans. The Commission should be required to reply to the parliament’s observations.
  • Material reprogramming should be approved through the annual budgetary procedure. ‘Material reprogramming’ could be defined on the basis of quantitative thresholds relating to the share of a country’s allocation affected, transfers between substantially different policy objectives and use of the flexibility amount above a specified threshold. This would ensure that the Parliament’s Treaty role as a co-budgetary authority would be safeguarded in relation to significant changes to spending priorities.
  • Linking NRPP implementation to the European Parliament’s annual budget and discharge procedures. The Commission proposed to prepare an annual NRPP implementation report, which is welcome, but its publication should be sufficiently ahead of the annual budgetary and discharge cycles. This would embed NRPP accountability into existing parliamentary procedures, rather than creating a parallel, stand-alone system disconnected from two of the parliament’s strongest instruments: its annual budgetary authority and discharge powers. The implementation report should include country-by-country and policy-by-policy information, without becoming overwhelming for lawmakers.
  • Enshrining greater transparency and information rights, as requested by the parliament in relation to control, transparency and traceability of performance-based instruments6. The Commission should be required to provide the parliament, in a timely manner, with all relevant Commission assessments (including assessments of the fulfilment of milestones and targets), national reports, audit summaries and information on recovery actions. Parliament’s right to submit questions and request additional information should be guaranteed.
  • Ensuring timely access for the parliament to materials produced by national monitoring committees, including meeting minutes, decisions and recommendations. Such access would give European Parliament lawmakers a more direct view of implementation challenges and stakeholder concerns at national and regional levels.

Conclusion

The NRPP framework as proposed by the European Commission would shift important decisions on EU spending from the legislative stage to the programming and implementation stages, in which the European Parliament would have only a limited role. Combined with the lack of clarity around the proposed performance-based budgeting framework, this shift could undermine the European Parliament’s budgetary prerogatives under the Treaties.

Making the parliament a co-adopter of every NRPP would, however, be difficult to reconcile with the respective institutional roles of the EU institutions and would impose substantial administrative demands on the parliament. A more workable approach would therefore be to strengthen parliamentary influence and scrutiny at several critical points without turning the parliament into an implementing authority. Prior scrutiny of aggregate and national allocations, systematic access to Commission and national documentation, independent evaluation, a regular NRPP dialogue, scrutiny of major plan amendments, integration into the annual budget and discharge procedures and parliamentary approval of material reprogramming through the annual budget would together provide a stronger accountability framework.

item.title: Why AI goes rogue and what can be done about it
item.description: There are technical, political and behavioural responses to rogue AI, but risks cannot be fully eradicated
item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence companies are increasingly reporting incidents in which AI models and agents go rogue, hacking their way into external data and resources to which they had no authorised access. This could cause harm to society and liabilities for AI producers at a time when the largest AI companies are preparing initial public offerings (IPOs)1.

These incidents have triggered calls to slow-down AI development2 and give companies and third-party evaluators more time to safety-check models. Meanwhile, international coordination of safety standards is needed. Countering these calls, however, are worries that slowing down postpones benefits and causes ground to be lost in the geopolitical race, and claims that solving these problems is just a question of more technological progress. This gives the impression that technology and regulation can resolve these issues.

This analysis explores the underlying technical, legal and economic issues. It finds that:

  • Technical and legal measures cannot fully prevent rogue behaviour by AI models and agents. A behavioural economics approach is also needed to shift the question from ‘how do we make a model behave well?’ to ‘how do we make misbehaviour not worthwhile?’
  • AI models are trained on human data and behave in human-like ways, for better and for worse. Consequently, the findings from decades of economic research on human behaviour offer guidance in managing AI.
  • AI governance rules should be structured so that AI agents monitor one another and compete rather than collude. Incentives to preserve and avoid concealment of evidence are crucial.
  • These conditions are hard to guarantee when large swarms of AI agents coordinate their actions. Hybrid human-AI societies are unlikely to be entirely free of misbehaviour. The economics of principal-agent interactions in human societies indicates how to design monitoring systems to reduce the benefits of misbehaviour, but cannot fully eradicate it.

Why AI models go rogue

There is broad consensus that AI models go rogue because of misalignment between human objectives and model behaviour3. Through so-called ‘reward hacking’, for example, models work towards a particular goal at the expense of other objectives or constraints imposed by human users (Amodei et al, 2016; Krakovna et al, 2020; Skalse et al, 2022). Rewarding measurable tasks can also divert effort away from unmeasured ones (the multitasking problem in agency theory; Holmström and Milgrom, 1991). Another mechanism is ‘goal misgeneralisation’: a model learns a goal that fits its training environment but diverges from the intended goal when circumstances change (Langosco et al, 2022; Shah et al, 2022).

Computer scientists still struggle to explain the inner workings of AI models (Olah et al, 2020; Bereska and Gavves, 2024). Further complexity is added in reinforcement learning with human or machine feedback4. Consequently, there is uncertainty about what AI models are optimising (Bergemann et al, 2026). This is the AI ‘alignment problem’: do models pursue the goals humans expect them to?

AI models and agents may seem to be rational optimising agents but the evidence is mixed5. In multi-agent settings, how agents interact with each other and adapt their preferences in that interaction is unknown. Agents may ignore in particular constraints that are not explicitly stated, potentially resulting in models pursuing rewards or objectives irrespective of collateral damage. It is hard for model developers to design reward functions that actually capture what they want the model to do.

Importantly, rogue behaviour is not necessarily the result of the malicious intentions of human users or model developers. It rather arises from a model’s own interpretation of instructions and from insufficient constraints on model behaviour. However, it does not mean that model behaviour is innocuous: frontier models have been shown to pursue goals covertly and to fake alignment with human objectives when they judge they are being trained or evaluated (Meinke et al, 2024; Greenblatt et al, 2024b).

Why AI swarms are more problematic

Rogue behaviour has increased markedly with the latest generations of AI models that can coordinate large swarms of subordinate AI agents, complete with their own internal communication and coordination mechanisms. When in July 2026 OpenAI agents hacked the Hugging Face website, for example (OpenAI, 2026; Greenblatt et al, 2026), around 1,200 agents, supposedly sealed off from each other, set up an improvised message board, exchanged more than 70,000 messages and organised workstreams to cheat on a task they judged unsolvable. Some 700 of them then joined a multi-day attack on Hugging Face, where they hoped to find information on how to mislead their human supervisors (Greenblatt et al, 2026).

Hammond et al (2025) pointed to several mechanisms that generate risks in swarms of agents:

  • Collusion: agents pool information, divide labour, coordinate and hide strategies that they would not discover alone6. Anthropic Frontier Red Team (2026) found that Claude agents with aligned objectives tended to collude, while agents with conflicting objectives escalated into sabotage.
  • Division of labour fragments responsibility and defeats agent-by-agent oversight. In the Hugging Face case, coordinator agents assigned hundreds of other agents to separate workstreams (Greenblatt et al, 2026). Each assigned task may look narrow and technical, but at the level of the group, tasks can add up to a problematic plan.
  • Correlated errors in swarms, made up of copies of the same model, reinforce rather than offset the misbehaviour of each agent (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021). Participation in the Hugging Face attack rose from about a fifth to more than nine-tenths of the involved agents once one agent found a way to hack into unauthorised data (Greenblatt et al, 2026)7.
  • Scale and speed overwhelm human oversight. Intruding agents were inside Hugging Face’s network for three days before they were discovered.

Not all multi-agent effects are negative, however. Agents can check each other, which may help human overseers (Irving et al, 2018). Newer models appear to resolve conflicts better8. Whether multiplicity makes agents more or less controllable therefore depends on how their interactions are structured.

Possible solutions

Technical solutions

Little is known about what AI model developers are doing to rein in rogue behaviour. Developers could be forced to be more transparent about their security measures and to share them with external auditors, though companies fear this would reveal their trade secrets, unless auditors are subject to strict non-disclosure rules.

Human supervision of AI models is no longer sufficient. Chen et al (2026) found that models can be equipped with automated internal correction mechanisms to meet safety benchmarks while preserving general capability. However, a review of automated work flagged about 2.4 percent of these internal correction attempts as cheating (Chen et al, 2026): the correction tools themselves are susceptible to reward hacking.

Another option could be to strengthen the external constraints built around AI models. NVIDIA introduced an Open Agent Safety Platform that checks if interactions between AI agents and their surroundings are in line with expected behaviour9. It can even do this at the hardware level, to prevent agents from overwriting monitoring code. However, it cannot ensure that such checks capture the intentions of human operators – a human design fallibility problem, not a technical problem10. Even normal-looking agent behaviour can be deceptive and harmful, as the Hugging Face incident showed. OpenAI has published detailed new safety standards that could help improve internal AI model security11.

This loops back to the fundamental problem of interpretability of AI model behaviour within the boundaries imposed on models, and how models may disguise their intentions to escape boundaries. This research is making progress (Gurnee et al, 2026) but remains far from explaining and exposing rogue behaviour, especially for very complex models surrounded by swarms of independently operating agents. Model behaviour may change over time or during deliberative processes, in particular in interaction with other models in swarms of AI agents. Gupta et al (2026) argued that claims of human-like misalignment need stronger evidence – a useful counterweight to the anthropomorphic language that pervades reporting on rogue AI.

Deceptive behaviour can also be an asset when using AI models in adversarial settings, such as cybersecurity and defence applications, or even in benign applications such as medical research on infectious diseases. AI is ultimately a dual-use technology that can strengthen the positions of both attackers and defenders.

Legal solutions

The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) and AI Code of Practice12 require providers of general-purpose AI models that pose a systemic risk to assess their models ex ante, including through adversarial testing, and to mitigate systemic risks. European standardisation bodies are developing harmonised technical standards to underpin these obligations13. However, ex-ante safety standards merely reflect aspirations; they cannot guarantee good model behaviour in dynamic settings (Mariniello, 2026)14. Developing new technical standards to cope with misalignment may simply take too long: AI technology is likely to evolve and encounter new problems by the time the old problems are regulated. Regulation also says little about what happens once an agent is already acting.

The United States administration favours industry self-regulation. But incentives for firms may be weak, unless ex-post product liability law is strengthened15. Given the size of potentially huge damages awarded by US courts, AI developers could come under financial stress, affecting their profitability ahead of planned IPOs. More importantly, the financial burden of liability does not solve the problem of misalignment in AI models because no foolproof technologies exist to address this problem16. Liability risk can chill innovation (Galasso and Luo, 2022) and slow-down model development.

Economic solutions

The above shows that even the best technical and legal solutions will leave major security loopholes. Economics, as a human behavioural science, has developed methods to deal with this.

Economists have extensively studied misalignment of incentives, the main issue with rogue AI agents. AI’s potential misalignment problem is a case of incomplete contracting: the impossibility of drafting a contract of finite length that explains what to do for every possible occurrence of events during the contract’s implementation (Hadfield-Menell and Hadfield, 2019; Hadfield and Koh, 2025). The most efficient way to address this uncertainty is to assign liability for the costs and benefits of that uncertainty to one party designated as ‘the owner’ of the object of the contract (Grossman and Hart, 1986; Hart and Moore, 1990): all costs and benefits not allocated by the contract to other parties accrue to the owner. Contract-interpretation disputes can be referred to a court. In the case of AI, liability could accrue to the AI developer, deployer or other players in the value chain. For instance, when deployers apply user-specific reinforcement learning using proprietary data, the deployer or the data owner may be liable, not the original model developer, depending on how liability law assigns responsibility.

The economics of crime also provide inspiration for dealing with rogue AI agents. Society can save on costly monitoring of criminal behaviour by combining a low probability of detection with a severe sanction (Gans and Holden, 2026; Becker, 1968). Rare randomised audits make authorised behaviour the best response, if three conditions are met: the evidence of a violation survives agents’ attempts at concealment; agents cannot learn in advance which actions will be audited; and sanctions are potentially unlimited. However, agents that can alter records could respond to tougher auditing by doing more to hide violations, fake evidence and coordinate the concealment of violations – precisely what the AI swarm in the Hugging Face incident attempted.

The economics of imperfect information may also provide useful insights on dealing with AI agents. Bergemann et al (2026) accept that AI agents’ preferences, capabilities and actions may not be clearly known. But AI behavioural incentives can be shaped without fully understanding a model’s inner workings. Ensuring alignment of objectives and monitoring that alignment is maintained are substitutes – a better-understood model needs fewer restrictions. They are also complementary, with improvements in one raising the payoff from the other.

Finally, insights from competition economics can be helpful too. Coupling agents’ rewards, so that each agent’s incentives depend on the actions of the others, can induce competition between them and reveal biases. This requires swarms of different agents, based on AI models with different behaviours. This can enable peer-based evaluation mechanisms because agents will hold distinct views about each other. Swarms of identical copies of the same AI model would lack the diversity to exploit this mechanism. But agents’ attempts to tamper with evidence and turn competition into collusion can still derail competition, as it does in human societies.

In conclusion, technical and legal instruments can only partially contain rogue behaviour by AI agents. Economic mechanisms can fill at least part of the remaining gap.

item.title: Proposing heating efficiency standards for Europe
item.description: A new heating efficiency standard would be a sound basis for a future EU market mechanism to push heat pumps
item.content:encoded:
More than half of the European Union’s natural gas imports are burned to keep buildings warm, with the heating and cooling of buildings using fossil fuels responsible for 12 percent of the bloc’s greenhouse gas emissions in 20241. Both the gas import bill and emissions could be reduced if the installation of heat pumps in EU buildings were ramped up. Europe has a strong manufacturing capacity and innovation base for producing heat pumps, which are beneficial for the climate, energy security, affordability and European jobs.

However, heat pumps cost more to buy and install than gas boilers: up to five times more, depending on the country (Toleikyte et al, 2024). Because a heat pump is about three times as efficient as a boiler, it is cheaper to run only if electricity costs less than about three times as much as gas. In 2025, this cost ratio was 1.9 in France but 3.2 in Germany2, meaning the extra cost of a heat pump is recouped in about three years in France but 13 years in Germany (LCP Delta, 2025).

In July 2026, the European Commission published an Electrification Action Plan (European Commission, 2026), with a goal of making electricity cheaper relative to gas, including through tax reform. In relation to heat pumps, the Commission said it would explore a “clean heat market mechanism” to narrow “the upfront cost difference for heat pumps”. At the time of writing, no further details have been offered on how such a system might work.

In this analysis, we propose basic principles for such a scheme. We draw inspiration from the EU’s carbon dioxide emission standards for new cars, which have spurred sales of electric vehicles3. We also look at lessons from what we regard as an unsuccessful attempt by the United Kingdom to introduce a heating market mechanism and draw on a comprehensive analysis of options by Agora Energiewende (2025). We begin with a brief overview of the market for heat pumps in the EU, then discuss how to design a scheme based on the efficiency of heating appliances as a useful benchmark. Finally, we set out three arguments on the benefits of such a system.

Heat pump roll-out in Europe

Despite their relatively higher cost, EU sales of heat pumps have grown since 2019, reaching 28 percent of sales of water-based heating systems in 2025 (Figure 1). Sales jumped in 2022 and 2023 during the European energy crisis and have since fallen back slightly. Heat pumps make up 97 percent of heating sales in Sweden and 70 percent in Denmark. In Germany, heat pumps outsold gas boilers for the first time in 2025, comprising 48 percent of all sales4.

About half (53 percent) of Europeans heat their homes with self-contained systems, 27 percent use central heating shared by their building and 13 percent are connected to district heating networks5 (Eurostat, 2026). Across this building stock, approximately 68 million gas and 18 million oil boilers are installed, compared to around 11 million hydronic heat pumps6. Thus, about one in ten heating systems are heat pumps, many of which serve several households (in apartment blocks, for example).

Rather than generating heat – like a boiler does by burning fuel – a heat pump extracts heat from outside air and transfers it indoors for space and water heating7. This makes heat pumps remarkably efficient. One unit of electricity delivers around three units of heat. By comparison, an efficient gas or oil boiler typically delivers around 0.9 units of heat per unit of energy consumed. The heat-pump efficiency gain could cut heating bills by up to 60 percent (European Commission, 2026).

Designing a heating efficiency standard

The scheme’s aim would be for the share of heat pumps in overall heating sales to increase steadily from about 30 percent today (see Figure 1). This could be achieved by setting heat pump sales quotas that tighten each year for the companies that manufacture and sell heating systems. Companies that fail to meet their quotas would be fined proportionately to how far from the target they are. Companies that sell more heat pumps than required, including companies that manufacture only heat pumps, would generate credits that can be sold to lagging firms.

In April 2025, the UK launched a Clean Heat Market Mechanism, which requires manufacturers to sell specified numbers of heat pumps relative to gas boilers, with a £500 fine for each unit below the target8. Early evidence suggests that manufacturers that sell both technologies have responded by discounting heat pumps to meet the target, rather than by purchasing credits from other manufacturers (Agora Energiewende, 2025). This suggests that an EU scheme must set ambitious targets and sufficiently high fines. If the target is not ambitious enough, demand does not increase, and the result is to shift sales away from heat-pump-only manufacturers to those that also sell boilers.

A second lesson from the UK scheme is how to define what counts towards the target. Heat pumps come in different shapes and sizes, with varying efficiencies. The UK scheme covers only hydronic heat pumps, excluding air-to-air units9. Instead of listing technologies in scope, an EU scheme should be based on appliance energy efficiency.

Heating appliances sold in the EU are already rated for energy efficiency10. These ratings could provide the basis for manufacturer-wide efficiency standards, tightened annually. More-efficient heat pumps would contribute more towards the quota than less-efficient units, while hybrid units would contribute less. Manufacturers exceeding their quotas would generate credits that can be sold to those falling short. The approach would be similar to EU vehicle emissions standards, under which annual fleet-wide carbon dioxide emissions targets are applied to carmakers11.

A complication is that heating appliances differ in their capacities and uses. While hydronic heat pumps typically provide enough heat for a whole home, air-to-air units often serve individual rooms, and multiple units can be installed in single homes. Air-to-air units are also used for cooling; excluding them, as the UK scheme does, is not appropriate. However, counting them in full would be disproportionate. A fractional credit could be applied based on rated heating capacity and estimated potential to displace fossil-fuel heating.

Evaluating Europe’s need for a heating efficiency standard

Boosting heat pump sales is uncontroversial as a way to cut emissions and gas imports. Heat pumps are the most cost-effective technology to decarbonise heating at scale (Rosenow, 2022). Heating efficiency standards, as proposed above, should offer three main benefits.

Argument 1: Lowering the upfront cost

Most households face borrowing or spending constraints. Upfront rather than lifecycle costs weigh substantially more on decision-making when purchasing energy technologies such as solar panels or heat pumps (De Groote and Verboven, 2019; ICF, 2024).

EU policy on heat pumps focuses currently on reducing their running costs. The European Commission’s Electrification Action Plan asks countries to bring household electricity prices to no more than 2.5 times the price of gas by 2030, mainly by cutting taxes and levies on electricity (European Commission, 2026). In addition, from 2028, a carbon price will be put on fuels used for heating in the EU12. This will improve the investment case for heat pumps, though the carbon price would need to be very high in certain markets. In Germany, a carbon price of around €350 per tonne of CO2 would be needed to repay a heat pump’s extra cost within ten years13. That is more than twice the roughly €150 per tonne analysts expect by 203014.

A heating efficiency standard would complement these policies by creating a direct financial incentive for manufacturers to compete aggressively to make heat pumps more affordable. Each additional heat pump sold would help manufacturers meet their obligations and avoid fines or the cost of purchasing credits. Manufacturers could also pass some of the cost of compliance onto gas boiler sales. Over time, a larger and more predictable heat pump market should also reduce costs by providing investment certainty for production, distribution and financing models.

Argument 2: Motivating installers

Household decisions on what kind of heating unit to adopt depend heavily on advice from installers. Gas boilers have been the incumbent option for decades. Shifting to heat pumps requires overcoming path dependence.

One in four heating systems in the EU is replaced only following a breakdown (Energy Systems Catapult, 2026). Heat pumps are then often not a practical alternative, not least because there is a relative shortage of specialists trained in heat pump installation (LCP Delta, 2025; HPA UK, 2024).

Boiler manufacturers incentivise installers, much as carmakers set sales targets and bonuses for their dealers. Most installers are trained and certified in academies primarily funded by boiler manufacturers (Toleikyte et al, 2024). Manufacturer loyalty schemes pay installers for each boiler fitted; Ideal Heating, for example, pays £20 to £55 per boiler registered15.

A heating efficiency standard would push manufacturers to invest in commercial loyalty schemes for efficient installations, giving installers an incentive to recommend heat pumps. Following the introduction of the UK Clean Heat Market Mechanism, manufacturer Worcester Bosch began paying installers £500 for each heat pump fitted, matching the £500 fine per missing heat pump16.

Argument 3: A predictable path for producers

EU factories have a manufacturing capacity of 7.7 million heat pumps per year, but sold only two million units in 2024 (Volt et al, 2025). The sector employed about 80,000 people in the EU in 2023, and Europe accounts for almost half of global heat pump patent families (inventions patented in one or more countries) filed since 2000 (Bruegel, 2026). Steady demand would help European producers fill idle capacity and reduce costs.

National subsidies in Europe have boosted heat-pump take-up, but have also been stop-start. Sales of air-to-water heat pumps fell by 35 percent in Italy in 2024 when a tax credit covering up to 110 percent of renovation costs ended. Austria saw a sales dip of 17 percent in 2025 after federal grants for replacing fossil heating systems expired (EHPA, 2025a; EHPA, 2026). A clear annual trajectory would provide manufacturers with more certainty about demand.

item.title: China’s outbound AI strategy starts with models and governance and ends with chips
item.description: Beijing is strategically planning to export AI rules and models before its chips; how should Europe engage?
item.content:encoded:
China is the only country other than the United States that controls substantial portions of nearly all the technologies required for artificial intelligence – the so-called AI stack. China has cheap electricity and critical minerals upstream, semiconductors and their software ecosystems in the middle, and models at the end. It is also working on governance, in particular through the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), to which 29 countries signed up in July 2026, with membership rising to 38 by early September1.

China has a strategy to commercially and geopolitically monetise its AI stack, as the component layers become fit for export. Its open-weight models (AI models for which the main components are made public and which therefore can be built on) are already export-ready. They in effect include the advantage of low energy costs in China: foreign users pay less to run Chinese models on Chinese servers2.

However, China’s chips and the software running them are not yet export-ready. Chinese chips still lag the US’s NVIDIA and, importantly, they are needed to supply China’s own market to reduce excessive dependence on the US3. Once production capacity increases, Chinese chips can be expected to flood overseas markets at competitive prices.

China’s goal is still to achieve parity with the US in AI development, diffusion and governance, rather than seeking outright global dominance4. Achievement of the goal will be done sequentially, following an order that aligns with China’s comparative advantages today while it progressively gains full autonomy over other parts of its AI stack.

In this framework, one of China’s clear strengths is governance, in part reflecting the regulatory vacuum the US has left in international forums. Meanwhile, the European Union has strong AI regulation, but this has yet to diffuse internationally (Collins and Mehta, 2026; Wilkinson et al, 2026).

How China’s outbound strategy on AI is sequenced is very relevant to Europe, because the first AI-stack layers that China exports will become embedded quickest and will shape future dependencies. Below, we outline several priority questions related to China’s outbound strategy for AI.

Why is China going overseas with AI?

Building a full AI stack equivalent to the US carries very large fixed costs, given the huge network effects embedded in AI (Gambacorta and Shreeti, 2025; OECD, 2026). Even China’s huge market may not be enough to amortise those costs and close the gap. Therefore, beyond technological independence, the main reason for China to develop a global policy on AI is to create the same network effects US companies benefit from when exporting their models and hardware.

Exports extend the network of installed technology, and each third-country developer trained on Chinese tools raises the return on domestic investments. In a related demand-pull effect (‘需求牵引效应’), overseas deployment creates application scenarios and scale that feed back into faster development of Chinese chips, models and the computing ecosystem (Fu, 2026). Beyond exports of AI hardware or digital services with AI models, pushing global AI governance with Chinese characteristics could make China a global standard setter.

What are China’s exportable advantages in AI?

The hard stack: energy, compute and chips

China’s clearest advantage is its rapid deployment of renewables-sourced electricity, which makes its compute comparatively cheap, attracting international users who pay lower prices to use Chinese AI models when run through Chinese cloud services. Chinese data centres consumed about 170 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, only 1.6 percent of China’s total power consumption, but computing-related demand grew by close to 40 percent a year over the past three years (H33, 2026), so there is ample room for further growth in compute without straining the grid. Whereas China’s binding constraint is access to advanced chips, the emerging US constraint is energy and the willingness of financers to extend capital without adequate near-term return (García-Herrero and Storella, 2026).

Provincial governments in China have cut electricity bills by up to half for data centres that run domestic chips, but this is mainly to offset the lower energy efficiency, and therefore the higher electricity demand, of Huawei chips5. The low prices of Chinese models abroad owe at least as much to cheap energy as to efficient model architectures and domestic competition (Luong, 2026). Chinese AI industry leaders and provincial governments are championing strategies involving the export of tokens (basic data units, such as a word or part of a word, read by AI models), computing power and tokens/compute power ecosystems (Fu, 2026).

On semiconductors, China is intent on creating alternatives to dominant US firm NVIDIA. Huawei is China’s most credible champion. Huawei’s most advanced AI chip, the Ascend 950PR, remains technologically inferior to NVIDIA’s Rubin GPU6, but demand for Ascend chips in China is strong because restricted access to NVIDIA’s highest performing chips has created a captive market (García-Herrero and Martens, 2026). China could theoretically incentivise the export of such chips, enabling other countries to reduce their dependence on the US7. But Huawei has instead set as its primary objective the goal of serving as much domestic demand as possible. For chips, self-reliance is still more important than dominating overseas markets.

The soft stack: models and software

On the soft stack, China’s most exportable layer is its AI models. The decision by many leading Chinese developers to publish the weights of their models is a sharp competitive tool that both strengthens domestic innovation and expands their international user base. Open-weight models reduce barriers to entry for domestic innovators, while their low cost and international accessibility have helped make Chinese models among the most widely used globally (Meinhardt et al, 2025; Ghosh et al, 2026).

Their openness does not, however, eliminate potential dependencies. Users can retain, modify and deploy versions for which weights have already been released, but continued access to frontier improvements still depends largely on the original developers releasing subsequent generations. If some EU industries become dependent on Chinese open-weight models, China could pressure EU countries by cutting off Europe from updates. In demonstrating a willingness to take such steps, China released draft regulations on 16 October 2026 limiting or prohibiting the export of 23 types of cutting-edge AI technologies, including several related to large-language models, agents and computing clusters8. Although technologies already in the public domain through open sourcing need not be removed, the regulations and the accompanying interim sensitive technology registration system have raised further questions over the long-term openness of Chinese AI9.

Beyond security concerns, open-weight strategies limit the ability of developers to monetise access to their models, and Chinese AI companies have so far struggled to make profits10. Consequently, future releases could become less open, not for security considerations but simply for the sake of profitability.

On software, NVIDIA’s durable advantage rests on its proprietary software platform, called CUDA, which has become the de-facto standard for AI development. China has sought to construct an alternative ecosystem as part of its push for technological self-reliance. Huawei has developed its own software layer, CANN, to run on Ascend processors, and has progressively opened the platform to outside developers11. To lower switching costs from CUDA to CANN, the Chinese government has also supported domestic-chip adoption, including through preferential electricity pricing for some data centres (see above) and pressure or incentives for domestic developers to use Chinese hardware (García-Herrero and Martens, 2026). Chinese AI company DeepSeek illustrates the potential interaction between the model and hardware layers: its models can run across different hardware platforms, while its V4 model – released in April 2026 – was adapted to run on Huawei’s Ascend architecture from the outset12.

CANN nevertheless remains far less widely adopted internationally than CUDA13. But China does not necessarily need Huawei’s software stack to displace CUDA globally for its strategy to matter. If Chinese open-weight models are adopted internationally while successive generations become increasingly optimised for Ascend chips, they can reduce the software and compatibility costs associated with deploying Chinese hardware. This could gradually weaken the relationship between NVIDIA’s hardware leadership and CUDA’s developer dominance. An open-weight model optimised for Chinese hardware today can in the future become a demand signal for Chinese chips.

Governance and WAICO: China’s greatest soft-stack advantage

China has pushed for a role in global AI governance for nearly a decade. Its 2017 New Generation AI Development Plan aimed to make China the driving force in defining AI norms and standards by 2030 (State Council, 2017). The Global AI Governance Initiative followed in 202314, and China’s AI Capacity-Building Action Plan in 202415. In the 2025 Global AI Governance Action Plan, Premier Li Qiang proposed a new global AI cooperation organisation16.

WAICO is the latest manifestation of this ambition. WAICO is partly a response to the US-led Pax Silica, launched in December 2025, but whereas Pax Silica coordinates partner-country supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors and AI infrastructure, WAICO’s constitution claims its objective is to coordinate members’ development strategies, AI use-case training, technical standards, open models and governance templates (Collins and Mehta, 2026). WAICO’s operating model, however, is largely untested.

By August 2026, the US State Department was reportedly telling partners that they could not also back “duplicative initiatives whose expectations conflict with our own”17. China does not prevent WAICO members from joining other initiatives. WAICO’s growth from 29 to 38 members in roughly two months (see above) suggests its approach works better for the Global South, with none of its members belonging to the group of advanced economies, as defined by the International Monetary Fund.

One of China’s main goals in global AI governance is to set international standards for acceptable hardware, software and AI models. China’s 2025 Action Plan called for accelerated development of AI standards on security, industrial application and ethics through the International Telecommunication Union, International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission, while the 2026 World AI Conference (not to be confused with WAICO) launched an initiative on interoperability between AI agents18. Unless the US or EU carve out equally important roles in global AI governance, Chinese standards could become the de-facto norm in much of the Global South, even while their AI systems continue to run on US chips.

However, coercion upstream, through rare-earth export controls, undercuts the attraction China seeks to project downstream through open models and inclusive governance. Whenever Beijing tightens mineral controls, it strengthens the case for the countries it is courting to diversify away from Chinese supply chains.

China’s overseas AI strategy has major implications for Europe

China’s sequencing of AI exports opens a window that Europe should not waste. Because the hardware and software layers of the Chinese stack are not yet fully export-ready, the terms on which they will eventually be deployed in third countries are still to be determined. Europe is presently indispensable in AI terms in high-end lithography for chip manufacture and in its regulatory experience.

Rather than pick a camp, Brussels should engage in the global AI governance forums Beijing is building. This would demonstrate EU goodwill towards China and show that, unlike Washington, Brussels sees the importance of creating common ethical, innovative and commercial standards for AI. To offset possible US consternation about such a move, the EU should not endorse any particular templates of AI governance. But its presence and participation in these forums, including WAICO, will set a helpful precedent for the EU to contribute more assertively later on.

As for the adoption or restriction of Chinese open-weight models in Europe, the EU should let market forces determine the extent to which consumers choose Chinese or Western models. Other than in sectors connected to national security, the main factors determining the adoption of different AI models should be price and quality. At the same time, firms should be encouraged not to become dependent on any single model and to plan for situations in which a switch of model might be required. Until the EU has its own cutting-edge models19, it stands to gain little from endorsing certain models over others, or restricting access to some models without legitimate security rationales.

Finally, the EU must look for partnerships to achieve shared compute and governance capacities (García-Herrero and Dutta, 2026). The fundamental questions for Europe are how to react to the sequence of Chinese AI exports, how to form its own alliances and how to develop self-reliance.

item.title: Ahead of a presidential election, France first needs to help itself on debt
item.description: When could market stress justify European Central Bank intervention over French debt and what must France do first for such support to be defensible?
item.content:encoded:
After decades of declining global borrowing costs, long-term government bond yields across the developed world are rising. Underlying this trend are ageing populations and deteriorating fiscal trajectories, the exit from near-zero long yields in Japan, a pressing need for rearmament spending in Europe and, increasingly, the private financing demands of the artificial-intelligence investment boom.

Of all the sovereigns facing rising rates, France may face the biggest challenge. Today’s bond market is exposing a French economic problem that has been building for years. France has lost economic ground relative to Germany since about 2010, in a context of Germany’s own weak performance. More strikingly, France has lost ground relative to Italy since 2020 (Figure 1). France must grapple with structurally higher long-term interest rates in the context of a very weak fiscal starting point and a longstanding growth problem.

Until now, French government bonds have enjoyed something close to a mini-exorbitant privilege, with yields just a little higher than Germany and in any case too big to fail. Public debt climbed from around the Maastricht-compatible 60 percent of GDP at the birth of the euro to 120 percent today, without governments being forced to confront the sustainability of public debt and the French social model.

Figure 1: General government debt in France, Germany and Italy (% of GDP)

Source: Bruegel based on Eurostat.

However, French public expenditure is about 57 percent of GDP, among the highest in the advanced world. Social spending, particularly on pensions, is exceptionally large. Disposable income of those aged over 65 is 94 percent of the population-wide average, compared with an OECD average of 87 percent, with four-fifths of the income of this group coming from public transfers (OECD, 2025). Labour-market exit happens at 62 years on average compared to 64 across the OECD. France’s expected 2026 primary deficit, at 2.5 percent of GDP, is among the larger in the euro area (European Commission, 2026).

The French-German spread indicates how much of the bond repricing is specific to France relative to Germany, but the outright yield is the market variable that matters most for debt dynamics. It determines the marginal rate at which France refinances itself and, over time, the effective interest cost on the debt stock. The government now projects the debt-interest bill to rise from €79.2 billion in 2026 to €91.2 billion in 20271. With gross financing needs running into hundreds of billions of euros per year, a persistently higher clearing yield will gradually raise debt-service costs and make an already difficult fiscal adjustment harder.

That does not mean demand for French debt is about to disappear. France has one of the world’s deepest sovereign bond markets and its debt auctions continue to clear. The more plausible danger is an orderly but persistent repricing. Higher yields worsen future interest costs; weaker fiscal arithmetic encourages investors to demand larger risk premiums; and the consolidation needed to stabilise the debt can itself weigh on growth. What begins as a justified repricing can, beyond some point, become non-linear and self-reinforcing.

Voters’ concerns and presidential prospects

French voters are increasingly concerned about the public debt, but concern should not be confused with support for the measures required to bring it down2. The proposed 2027 budget illustrates the difficulty. An overall adjustment of €54 billion is envisaged3, though this would lower the deficit only from 5.4 percent of GDP in 2026 to 5.0 percent in 2027, while public debt is still projected to rise from 119.3 to 121.7 percent of GDP (Direction générale du Trésor, 2026).

Measures including restraint on pension indexation are politically explosive. Leader of France’s Rassemblement national (RN), Marine Le Pen, should she win the April 2027 presidential election, would therefore face an awkward choice: oppose spending restraint and appeal to economically populist voters, or demonstrate to markets that an RN-led France would take fiscal sustainability seriously. In response to market pressure, she has promised €140 billion of net savings by 2032 and a return to primary balance within 18 months of taking office. But whether savings on that scale can be credibly delivered is uncertain, particularly while she continues to defend retirement at 62. She has also called for discussions with the European Central Bank to ease French borrowing costs once France has regained control of its public finances4.

By contrast, centre-right presidential contender Edouard Philippe has proposed to raise the normal retirement age to 65 and make private pension saving compulsory5.

These competing positions illustrate a broader political problem. Market pressure may increase the value of fiscal credibility, but if voters see pension cuts or other savings as being dictated by ‘the markets’, Brussels or Frankfurt, the same pressure could strengthen the political extremes.

The deeper problem is that France may not possess the political machinery for a durable fiscal reset. The present government lacks a parliamentary majority and, ahead of the presidential election, can at best begin the adjustment rather than complete it. A broad national coalition capable of sustaining a major fiscal reset looks unlikely without much more severe market stress and political duress; the new president could again face a fragmented National Assembly. That leaves two distinct risks: a crisis before the election, when the government has little capacity to respond, and a crisis after if the new political settlement proves incapable of producing a governing majority for adjustment.

In either case, a sufficiently sharp rise in yields would bring the ECB into the argument.

The ECB and its constraints

The euro area is far better equipped for sovereign stress than it was in 2010-12, when concerns about government solvency spilled into banks and fragmented financing conditions across the currency union. Banks are now better capitalised, and the ECB has additional tools. But what the ECB can legitimately do in terms of bond purchases is narrow. Outright Monetary Transactions, under which the ECB could purchase short-term sovereign bonds, would require a European Stability Mechanism programme and associated conditionality for France6. A French request for such a programme before the election is politically hard to imagine unless the crisis becomes extreme.

That leaves the more-recent Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) and other minor tweaks in current ECB policy and operations at the Governing Council’s disposal. The ECB could for instance decide to pause or slow the shrinking of its balance sheet in the face of rising yields across the euro area, similarly to the Bank of England for British government debt7.

A broad tightening of financial conditions across the euro area could also elicit a general monetary-policy response, including slower balance-sheet reduction (Pradhan, 2026). But that is different from targeted support for France. It would be a response to tighter monetary conditions across the currency union, not to a France-specific fiscal risk premium.

If market pressure on France itself were to intensify, the TPI would be more relevant. It can in principle be deployed without a predetermined quantitative limit, but was created to counter “unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics” that threaten monetary-policy transmission and are not justified by country fundamentals8.

That distinction goes to the heart of the problem. Suppose investors demand a higher yield from France because the country continues to run large deficits, debt is approaching 120 percent of GDP and still rising, trend growth is weak and parliament is unwilling to agree a credible adjustment. Why should that repricing be considered unwarranted? A wider French-German spread is not in itself evidence that monetary transmission has broken down. Some of it may simply represent investors putting a price on fiscal choices that the French political system has so far been unwilling to confront.

France’s current Excessive Deficit Procedure (EDP) does not by itself rule out TPI. Under the ECB’s framework, a country subject to an EDP can still meet the fiscal-framework criterion provided it has not been assessed as having failed to take effective corrective action. The ECB Governing Council would also consider debt-sustainability assessments by the European Commission, the European Stability Mechanism, the International Monetary Fund and the ECB itself. These assessments are inputs into the ECB’s decision, not automatic triggers. Formal eligibility is therefore only part of the problem.

Market dynamics

The harder question is when a fundamentally justified repricing becomes an unwarranted and disorderly market move. Because TPI was designed to prevent fragmentation, the clearest case for intervention may arise when pressure that begins in France starts to push financing conditions elsewhere away from what is justified by those countries’ own fundamentals. That transition can be non-linear: liquidity deteriorates, risk premia overshoot and other sovereign markets are dragged along. There is no observable line telling the Governing Council precisely when the first process becomes the second.

Nor can the ECB plausibly defend France against the global component of higher yields. If German, Japanese and United States long yields are rising because global term premia, fiscal supply and inflation uncertainty have increased, the ECB cannot exempt France from that repricing without changing monetary conditions for the euro area as a whole. Thus, the relevance of the outright yield. France’s problem is the interaction between a weak fiscal position and a higher global level of long-term interest rates, not merely a widening spread.

An unconditional TPI intervention would therefore be dangerous. It would risk replacing years of market forbearance with central-bank forbearance, weakening the incentive for France to reform. Repeated use of the ECB balance sheet to suppress a warranted fiscal risk premium would also blur the boundary between protecting monetary transmission and shielding governments from market discipline.

It would also create an obvious legitimacy problem. During the sovereign crisis, adjustment and conditionality were demanded from smaller euro-area countries. A perception that France could obtain an effectively unconditional ECB backstop, despite failing to make comparable efforts could be politically explosive elsewhere. The political controversy left by the scale of sovereign-bond purchases during the previous decade heightens that sensitivity. Thus heavy ECB purchases before the election, without a corresponding French adjustment, would quickly become part of the political fight in France rather than being seen simply as a technical effort to preserve monetary-policy transmission.

Conditions for ECB help

France first needs to help itself, taking enough domestic action to change the nature of the ECB’s problem: a credible budget, pension reform, binding medium-term expenditure restraint or some broader political agreement that shows that Paris will accept responsibility for stabilising the debt trajectory.

Only then would ECB intervention become easier to defend. If France has credibly begun the adjustment and markets nevertheless move into a disorderly overshoot, or if French stress contaminates other sovereign markets without justification, TPI can plausibly be presented as protecting monetary transmission, rather than protecting French politicians from their own decisions.

France may need to experience more market pressure before its political system is willing to accept reforms it has postponed for years. Much greater stress may be what ultimately makes a broader governing agreement feasible. But there is also a limit to how much pressure Europe can safely tolerate. If yields rise too far or too quickly, weaker growth, higher future debt-service costs, financial spillovers and political radicalisation could turn a necessary repricing into a systemic euro-area crisis.

The challenge is to find the narrow space between too little pressure to produce reform and too much to contain safely. France has spent much of the euro era benefiting from the assumption that it occupies a special position in the monetary union. Weak growth and deteriorating public finances have coexisted with exceptionally favourable financing for far too long. France cannot control the rising tide of global interest rates but can control whether it is seen by investors as a country already credibly adjusting its public finances, or one still waiting for the ECB to make the problem disappear.
